topic: The journey of a drop of water
script: Every glass of water you drink has travelled further than you might think. Let us follow a single drop on its long journey around the planet. Our drop begins in the ocean, which holds about 97 percent of all the water on Earth. The sun warms the surface of the sea every day. Some of the water at the top turns into an invisible gas called water vapour. This step is called evaporation. The warm, moist air rises because it is lighter than the cool air around it. As it climbs, the air cools down. Cool air cannot hold as much vapour as warm air. So the vapour gathers on tiny specks of dust and salt. Billions of these small droplets together form a cloud. This step is called condensation. Our drop is now floating high above the sea, inside a white cloud. Winds carry the cloud across the coast and over the land. Inside the cloud, droplets bump into each other and join together. When they grow too heavy to float, they fall. This is precipitation. It can arrive as rain, snow, sleet or hail, depending on the temperature. Our drop falls as rain on a green hillside. Now it has three main choices. It can soak into the soil. It can run downhill across the ground. Or it can be taken up by the roots of a plant. Let us say our drop soaks into the soil. It sinks slowly between grains of sand and rock. Deep underground, it joins a large store of water called an aquifer. Water can stay in an aquifer for weeks, for centuries, or even for thousands of years. Our drop is patient. After many years it seeps out from a spring at the bottom of a valley. It joins a small stream, then a river. The river flows past fields, forests and towns. Along the way, people use some of the water for drinking, washing and growing food. Treatment plants clean the water before it reaches homes, and clean it again before it returns to the river. Plants play a quiet part in the journey too. A large tree can move hundreds of litres of water from the soil into the air on a hot summer day. Water climbs from the roots to the leaves and escapes through tiny pores. This is called transpiration. Some drops take a much colder route. Snow that falls on high mountains can be pressed into glaciers. A drop of water can stay frozen in a glacier for hundreds of years. In spring, part of the snow and ice melts and feeds the rivers below. Many cities depend on this meltwater through the dry summer months. Eventually, our river reaches the coast and pours into the sea. Our drop is back where it started, ready to rise again. The whole cycle has no beginning and no end. The same water has been moving around the Earth for billions of years. Only a tiny part of all the water on Earth is fresh water that we can easily use. That is why it matters to keep rivers clean and to use water carefully. Turning off a tap while brushing your teeth can save several litres every day. Fixing a dripping tap can save thousands of litres in a year. Every drop we save stays in the cycle for plants, animals and people. So the next time it rains, think of the long journey each drop has made. From the ocean to the clouds, from the hills to the rivers, and back to the sea again.
